title: Come Back, Unfaithful People
overview: Using the picture of a broken marriage, the LORD confronts his people's worship of other gods yet keeps calling both Israel and Judah to come home.

parts.label: A marriage beyond repair? (vv. 1-2)
parts.note: Israel's law said a man could not take back a wife he had divorced once she had married another man, and the LORD uses this to picture the people's worship of many gods at hilltop shrines. Translations differ on whether verse 1 ends as a shocked question or as a surprising invitation to return.

parts.label: Sweet words, same behavior (vv. 3-5)
parts.note: The spring rains that ripened the crops had failed, which was meant as a warning, yet the people showed no shame. In some translations they already call God 'Father' and ask him not to stay angry while still doing all the wrong they can, while in others God is inviting them to start calling him 'Father' from now on.

parts.label: Two unfaithful sisters (vv. 6-11)
parts.note: The northern kingdom of Israel, conquered and exiled by Assyria about a century before King Josiah, is pictured as a wife divorced for worshiping idols of stone and wood. Her sister Judah, the southern kingdom, watched this happen, did the same, and turned back only for show, so she is called the worse of the two.

parts.label: An invitation to come home (vv. 12-15)
parts.note: Jeremiah calls toward the north, where Israel's exiles had been taken, saying God will not stay angry if they simply admit what they have done. Even if only one from a town or two from a clan return, God promises to bring them to Jerusalem and give them good leaders.

parts.label: A future beyond the ark (vv. 16-18)
parts.note: The ark of the covenant was a sacred chest in the temple, seen as the place where God sat enthroned among his people. In this vision no one will even miss it, because all Jerusalem becomes God's throne, the nations come to honor him, and the divided north and south return home together.

parts.label: A confession at last (vv. 19-25)
parts.note: God had hoped to treat his people as his own children, and now weeping is heard on the very hilltops where they worshiped other gods. When he offers to heal them, they admit that this worship was a lie, and that the god they served, called here simply 'shame' (likely a mocking stand-in for the name Baal), devoured their herds and even their children, which may refer to child sacrifice.

disagreement: Christians differ on whether the promises of a reunited people gathered to Jerusalem (vv. 14-18) were fulfilled in the return from exile, are fulfilled spiritually in the church, or still await a future restoration of Israel.
think: Is there a point where broken trust can no longer be repaired, and if not, what would honest coming back actually look like?
